C1.rationale: Meets level 2 ('At least one core unit assesses collaborative practice — group projects with individual accountability, client or stakeholder work, interprofessional activity'): Screen Thinking 1's graded group presentation, Screen Making 1's collaborative production, and Screen Production's graded 'Collaborative practice participation and documentation' each assess teamwork. Level 3 additionally requires assessed coordination 'across people AND tools/AI systems' with the division of work itself assessed; the extract contains no AI or digital-tool content anywhere (see C3), so that clause is unmet.

C2.rationale: Meets level 2 ('core assessment includes criterion-referenced appraisal of quality: peer review, structured critique...'): Screen Story 1's graded structural script-analysis presentation requires students to 'critically interpret the work of a writer.' Level 3 requires assessment documenting/justifying reliance decisions or evidencing 'strategy adjustment over time (process-focused assessment)'; Screen Thinking 1's graded 'Individual methodology paper,' tied to evaluating 'their own process ... to define a working methodology of practice,' gestures toward this but does not clearly document adjustment over time or reliance/override decisions — ambiguous, held at the lower level per the scoring-direction rule.

Individual methodology paper

C3.rationale: No unit among the seven fully-documented core subjects references AI or digital tools. The nearest content, Screen Thinking 2's outcome to 'evaluate and contextualise technological and content innovations' and to 'critically evaluate the disruption of the film value chain model,' addresses industry disruption generally rather than AI or digital-tool use, limitations, ethics or governance, so it does not clear even level 1 ('AI or digital tools appear only as electives or as tool operation/training'). Scored 0 against the documented core (see ambiguities re: the undocumented specialisation-linked core subjects).
evidenceLines: evaluate and contextualise technological and content innovations spanning the global screen industry;
critically evaluate the 'disruption' of the film value chain model and its impact on the screen industry;

C4.rationale: Meets level 3 ('a self-scoped capstone or research project'): Screen Story 2 has students develop 'screen ideas and creative treatments ... for screen productions they may produce in their capstone subject, Screen Production,' and Screen Production has them 'prepare, re-draft, analyse and finalise the screen idea they developed in Screen Story 2' while leading 'a creative team in the realisation of a substantive short screen work' — a self-originated project carried through and assessed at the capstone via the graded Creative project folio, satisfying R2's assessment requirement.

C5.rationale: Practice-led research is named at program level and in Screen Production's generic skills, which under R2 caps the item at 1 absent clear assessed evidence of 'design[ing] and conduct[ing] an inquiry with methodology selection and data collection.' Screen Post-Production's graded 'creative methodology/process oral presentation' and Screen Thinking 1's graded 'Individual methodology paper' name assessed methodology deliverables that could support level 2, but both read as reflection on the creative/production process rather than a designed inquiry with data collection — ambiguous, held at the lower level.
evidenceLines: critically engage with practice-led research principles and methods in creating screen work;

W1.rationale: Meets level 2 ('a recognised professional genre ... — client brief, consultancy or policy advice ... pitch'): Screen Story 1's graded '5-minute video story pitch' and Screen Story 2's graded '15-minute story pitch / oral presentation' are pitches, a genre the anchor names directly. Level 3 requires progression AND delivery to/judgement by a real external audience or practitioner with conduct explicitly assessed; Screen Production's Production Compliance hurdle clearly assesses professional conduct/accountability, and Screen Post-Production's work is completed 'in preparation for public exhibition' while Screen Production names 'industry mentors' as interlocutors — but no single assessed item is unambiguously delivered to or judged by that external audience rather than the teaching team, so this is ambiguous between 2 and 3; held at the lower level.

Hurdle requirement: To meet the requirements necessary for authorisation to commence shooting their film projects, students must submit all required production and compliance paperwork during scheduled meetings. This documentation is crucial for achieving the Film Department's sign-off and must include, but is not limited to, location agreements, cast agreements, and script approvals. Submission of these documents at designated intervals is mandatory and serves as a hurdle requirement for progressing to the shooting phase of their projects.
Students will research and apply knowledge through creative reflection, analysis of production and post-production choices to complete their screen work in preparation for public exhibition.
critically engage in creative conversations about ethics, aesthetics and story with lecturers, peers and industry mentors;

W2.rationale: Meets level 3 ('such tasks are the program's assessment spine ... AND at least one carries a genuine constraint of practice'): the program scaffolds practitioner artefacts across its core — Screen Story 1's graded 'Short screenplay or treatment,' explicitly produced to industry-standard formatting, and Screen Making 1's graded 'Scheduling and budget exercise based on a short film script' — culminating in Screen Production's capstone, which requires 'delivering a film to budget and to schedule' and compliance with 'industry-standard screen production processes and documentation,' a genuine resource/time constraint of practice.
